Where it began

Prasidh Krishna was born in Bengaluru on 19 February 1996 and studied at JAIN University.

He made his first-class debut for Karnataka in September 2015, against a touring Bangladesh A side, at a time when all three of the state's leading quicks were missing. He needed only one ball to make his mark, removing Rony Talukdar, and three more wickets in that opening spell left the visitors 41 for 5. He finished with 5 for 49 and Karnataka won by four wickets.

The player

A right-arm fast-medium bowler, he rose through the Karnataka one-day side, where he led their wicket-takers in the 2018–19 Vijay Hazare Trophy, and on to India A and the Emerging Teams Asia Cup. His first ten-wicket haul in first-class cricket came in the 2021–22 Ranji Trophy against Jammu and Kashmir, with 6 for 35 and 4 for 59.

His ODI debut, against England in March 2021, brought four wickets, the most any Indian had taken on ODI debut, and India won by 66 runs. His Test debut followed at Centurion against South Africa. By November 2026 he had played 9 Tests for India and taken 32 wickets at 30.34, with a best of 4 for 62. In the 2025 Anderson-Tendulkar Trophy against England he was picked for three of the five Tests and took 14 wickets.

What made him special

Pace, persistence and a knack for taking wickets in clusters. Against the West Indies in 2022 he took 4 for 12 in an ODI and was named player of the series, and he was part of the squad that won the 2023 Asia Cup and reached the final of that year's World Cup.

Batting was less his department. By November 2026 he had made 18 Test runs at 2.57, with a best of 5 not out, though he was not out in six of his 13 innings, so nobody could say he gave his wicket away cheaply.

Away from the middle

He has been a regular in the IPL, starting with Kolkata Knight Riders in 2018, moving to Rajasthan Royals in 2022 and on to Gujarat Titans in 2025. That last season was a fine one: his 25 wickets earned him the Purple Cap as the leading wicket-taker of the tournament.

And finally

A wicket with your first ball in first-class cricket and a national record on your ODI debut is not a bad way to start. Most bowlers spend years waiting for a first impression like that. He managed two.
